intro: Grieg plays a two-minute version of his own wedding-anniversary march, recorded in Paris in 1903. Short chords, low D octaves and quick triplets give the tune a spring in its step.

sections.label: A · The D major march
sections.mNote: Low octaves and clipped chords set the march going

sections.label: B · The march continues
sections.mNote: Quick triplets lift the piano melody

sections.label: C · Chords across the keyboard
sections.mNote: The march fills out in octaves and chords

sections.label: D · The shortened close
sections.mNote: Grieg brings his two-minute version to an end

cues.title: The composer at the piano
cues.text: Low D octaves alternate with clipped chords. A quick triplet lifts the melody into the march. Grieg marks the opening Tempo di Marcia un poco vivace: a march with a little life in it. Here the hands at the keyboard are his own.
cues.evidence: Grieg, Op. 65 No. 6, bars 1–10, Louis Oesterle edition, typeset by David Whipple for Mutopia: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/GriegE/O65/troldhaugen/troldhaugen-a4.pdf. Grieg’s Paris session of 2 May 1903, matrix 2149F: https://www.marstonrecords.com/products/legendary-piano
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: More guests than expected
cues.text: Grieg writes the piece in the summer of 1896, remembering his silver wedding anniversary at Troldhaugen. Far more guests arrive than the couple have invited. His first title is “The well-wishers are coming”. The piano makes a fine welcoming band.
cues.evidence: Ernst-Günter Heinemann and Einar Steen-Nøkleberg, preface to Henle HN 1291 (2016), pp. III–IV: composition date, silver wedding and autograph title “Die Gratulanten kommen”, translated here. https://www.henle.de/media/cb/cd/75/1697725893/1291-1697725893-sync.pdf

cues.title: Grieg is glad to leave
cues.text: Eleven days after the recording, Grieg writes from Leipzig to Julius Röntgen: “I was glad to say farewell to France, and especially Paris.” The visit leaves nine short piano recordings behind, including this compressed celebration of home.
cues.evidence: Grieg to Julius Röntgen, Leipzig, 13 May 1903, quoted in Marston’s Legendary Piano Recordings booklet; the same essay documents nine sides recorded in Paris on 2 May. https://www.marstonrecords.com/products/legendary-piano

composer.epithet: The Bergen merchant’s son who put Norwegian fiddle tunes, a troll king and a wedding party into concert-hall music.
facts: Conductor in Christiania, 1866–74 · Harmonien, Bergen, 1880–82 · a state composer’s stipend from 1874
Rikard Nordraak 1864–65 · Piano Concerto 1869 · Peer Gynt 1876 · Troldhaugen 1885
Ten books of Lyric Pieces, about 170 songs, a piano concerto, stage music, a string quartet and five sonatas

quote.text: The most important thing is truth, the truth of feeling.
quote.source: Grieg to Julius Röntgen, May 1904, quoted in Finn Benestad, Norsk biografisk leksikon

composer.background:
Edvard Grieg was born on 15 June 1843 in the family house at Strandgaten 152, above Bergen’s harbour. His father, Alexander, was a merchant and the British vice-consul; his mother, Gesine, who had studied singing, piano and theory in Hamburg, taught him the piano from the age of six. He hated scales. What he remembered, in his essay Min første Succes, was the day at five when he stretched up to the keyboard and found a third, a triad, a four-note chord and at last, with both hands, the five notes of a ninth. “That was a success!” he wrote. “Nothing since has been able to intoxicate me like this.”

In the summer of 1858 the violinist Ole Bull called without warning at the Griegs’ summer house at Landås. Edvard was made to play. Bull grew serious, talked quietly with the parents, then shook the boy in his own way and said: “You are going to Leipzig to become an artist!” On 6 October Grieg entered the Conservatory. He later called it “that damned Leipzig conservatory”, yet he went free to the Gewandhaus rehearsals, saw Tannhäuser fourteen times, and heard Clara Schumann play her husband’s concerto. In the spring of 1860 tuberculosis ruined one of his lungs. That autumn, against the doctor’s advice, he went back.
